name: Cancel Amazon Prime
shortDescription: One membership, six businesses you're also funding.
longDescription: Prime bundles retail, logistics, cloud, advertising and media into a single recurring charge. Cancelling is an account setting, not a boycott of every seller who happens to list there — and it stops the part of the bill that funds the bundle.

name: Delete the Amazon app from your phone
shortDescription: Removes the two-tap path from idle thumb to checkout.
longDescription: Most impulse orders come from the app, not the website. Deleting it doesn't close your account — it just puts a browser and a login between you and the purchase, which is enough friction to break the habit.

name: Remove your saved card from one online retailer
shortDescription: One-click buying only works if the card is already there.
longDescription: Stored payment details are the whole design of frictionless retail. Deleting the card from one retailer's account means the next purchase is a decision rather than a reflex. Repeat it per retailer.

name: Buy your next book from an independent bookshop
shortDescription: Same book, and the margin stays in your town.
longDescription: Independent bookshops order most titles within a couple of days, and many run their own online shops. The book costs about the same; the difference is which balance sheet it lands on.

name: Switch one cleaning brand off P&G or Unilever
shortDescription: Detergent, dish soap, surface spray. Decided once, bought for years.
longDescription: A handful of conglomerates own most of the cleaning aisle. Pick one product you rebuy on autopilot and change the default — the switch only has to be made once, but it repeats every time the cupboard empties.

default: an independent or cooperative household brand

name: Switch your personal care brand
shortDescription: Shampoo, toothpaste, deodorant — same shelf, different owner.
longDescription: Personal care is one of the most concentrated aisles in the shop. Changing one product you buy monthly redirects a small amount reliably, which is worth more than a large one-off.

name: Move your regular shop to a cooperative grocer
shortDescription: The weekly shop is the largest recurring number most people control.
longDescription: Groceries go on autopilot to whichever shop is nearest or already in an app. Changing the default — to a co-op, a regional chain, a food cooperative — redirects a recurring amount rather than a single purchase. This one is worth checking in on, because defaults drift back.

name: Buy your next device refurbished instead of new
shortDescription: A phone that already exists doesn't book a new unit sale.
longDescription: Refurbished marketplaces sell graded, warrantied devices at a discount. The manufacturer records no new sale, and the device that would have been built isn't. Warranties are typically 12–24 months.

name: Replace one US soft drink brand for good
shortDescription: The most replaceable recurring purchase in the shop.
longDescription: Soft drinks are bought by habit and brand recall, and nearly every European market has an independent cola or lemonade with a real following. This is the lowest-friction permanent swap on the list.

default: a local or independent soft drink brand

name: Buy it secondhand instead of new
shortDescription: Clothes, furniture, tools — the resale market is enormous and local.
longDescription: Secondhand purchases move money between people rather than to a manufacturer. Most European countries have a dominant local marketplace that isn't US-owned.

name: Skip a US fast-food chain for a local place
shortDescription: Same lunch, and the money stays within a few streets.
longDescription: Fast food is the most franchised category there is, and a franchise fee leaves the local economy on every order. The independent equivalent is usually the same price and closer.

name: Unsubscribe from one retailer's marketing emails
shortDescription: Cuts the prompt that generates the purchase.
longDescription: Retail email exists to manufacture a purchase occasion you weren't going to have. One unsubscribe link removes a recurring nudge permanently, and under GDPR the retailer has to honour it.

name: Shop at your local market this week
longDescription: Market traders and producers keep a far larger share of what you hand over than a supermarket supply chain passes back. Once a week is a meaningful recurring redirect.

name: Cancel a warehouse club membership
shortDescription: An annual fee for the privilege of spending more.
longDescription: Warehouse memberships charge up front and then rely on bulk purchasing to justify themselves. Cancelling ends both the fee and the sunk-cost pull to keep shopping there.
